summary: Summarizes requirements for gateways on networks that use the DARPA Internet protocols. Though aimed at National Science Foundation research programs, it gives vendors general guidance, listing the protocols gateways must support and the documents that describe them. It was a draft and was replaced by RFC 1009.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a checklist for companies building the machines that connect networks together, saying what rules those machines must know.

subtitle: A May 1986 draft checklist of what a vendor's Internet gateway must support, written for NSF networks but meant for everyone.

tldr.problem: Vendors were building gateways for networks running the DARPA Internet protocols, and the existing specifications were scattered, evolving, and sometimes ambiguous or incomplete.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists the protocols a gateway must implement and points to the RFCs that define them. It adds guidance where those specifications are unclear, covering routing, local network interfaces and remote operation.
tldr.outcome: It was a draft that asked for comments for 90 days, and it was obsoleted by RFC 1009.

facts.label: Failover target
facts.value: Less than the typical TCP user timeout (one minute assumed)

today: RFC 985 was a draft, and it was obsoleted by RFC 1009, so it is no longer the current statement of gateway requirements. Its status is listed as Unknown.

sections.title: The Gateway Model and Its Audience
sections.content:
RFC 985 was prepared by the Gateway Requirements Subcommittee of the NSF Network Technical Advisory Group. It applies specifically to National Science Foundation research programs, but its requirements are stated generally and are believed applicable throughout the Internet community. Its purpose is to give guidance to vendors whose products might be used in an Internet application.

An Internet gateway is described as a self-contained, stand-alone packet switch. It interfaces to two or more packet-switching networks, conforms to the specified protocols, supports an interior gateway protocol where several gateways operate as a system, forwards datagrams with good management of resources, congestion and fairness, and provides system support facilities such as loading, debugging and status reporting.

The memo names three typical scenarios: a national or regional network, a campus network and a department network. They differ in how much traffic they switch. The regional case is expected to handle continuous flows in the 1.5-Mbps range and the campus and department cases burst flows at 10-Mbps. Gateways normally run unattended, so they must be highly robust and keep working, possibly degraded, under extreme congestion or failure.
sections.plainLanguage: A gateway is a junction that joins different networks. The memo says a junction for a big region needs to be very fast, and a small one for a single department can be simpler, but all of them must keep working without anyone watching.

sections.title: Protocols a Gateway Must Support
sections.content:
The memo lists four protocols and assumes the full protocol is implemented, including required options, except where it says otherwise. They are the Internet Protocol (IP), the Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP), the Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP, described in RFC 904) and the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP).

For IP, the Type of Service field and the Security, Stream ID and Timestamp options may be ignored for now, but if they are recognized they must be interpreted as the standard says. A gateway need not reassemble datagrams addressed to other hosts. Class-D and Class-E addresses are reserved for experiments, so a gateway not taking part should ignore packets sent to them and should not send ICMP Destination Unreachable or Redirect messages for them.

For ICMP, the memo recommends avoiding the network-level Destination Unreachable and Redirect messages, because the span of addresses they imply is ill-defined when a sender does not know the subnet mask. Gateways should instead send a Destination Host Unreachable message for each distinct unreachable address, and prefer host redirects. New implementations are expected to support the ICMP Address Mask messages from RFC 950. The memo says it is not realistic to specify when Source Quench should be generated or interpreted.

On EGP, the memo notes that only the non-core procedures were specified, that there were no peer-discovery or authentication procedures, and that using EGP as a general routing algorithm is discouraged because implementations adapt slowly and have no loop protection. A gateway running its own routing algorithm must declare a net down via EGP when its routing algorithm does.
sections.plainLanguage: Every junction must speak a small set of shared languages. The memo says which ones, and warns about a few messages that can confuse people if used carelessly.

sections.title: Subnets, Local Networks and Interoperability
sections.content:
The memo asks that each network interface have a (sub)net address and an address mask, set during configuration. It should be possible to add gateways or subnets, or make other configuration changes, without taking the whole network down.

It then summarizes how datagrams are carried on each kind of local network: public data networks via X.25, the ARPANET via 1822 or via DDN Standard X.25, Ethernets, and serial lines. On Ethernet, datagrams are encapsulated with 48-bit source and destination addresses and a 16-bit type field, and ARP is required. The IP broadcast address has an all-ones host field, and early implementations that used all-zeros do not conform to RFC 950. For serial lines, no particular protocol is required, but standard hardware and protocols are recommended, ideally some variation of full X.25.

To make gateways from different vendors work together, the memo defines points of protocol demarcation. For routing, it is EGP. At the network layer and below, there is one point for Ethernets and one for serial lines. All gateway systems must include one or more gateways that support EGP with a core gateway. Appendix A adds detailed Ethernet rules on when to accept or discard IP datagrams, ARP messages and ICMP redirects.

Appendix B says NSF gateways must support an Ethernet attachment to gateways of other vendors, whatever proprietary switching technology they use inside.
sections.plainLanguage: Different towns use different kinds of roads. The memo says how traffic is packed for each road type, and picks one common road, Ethernet, where junctions from different makers must be able to meet.

sections.title: Reachability and Routing
sections.content:
Gateways that act as general packet switches in a network of modest size need extra functions. The architecture must be able to establish whether each link and node is working, usually with periodic hello messages across each link. The memo warns that a working link-level protocol does not prove the host or gateway behind it works, so a routing algorithm or a peer-level reachability protocol such as EGP should confirm it. Failures and restorations must be reported to the control center.

The memo says repeated Internet experience shows routing to be the single most important engineering issue in network design. It lists features it considers necessary. The algorithm must detect link or gateway failure or restoration and switch paths in less than the typical TCP user timeout (one minute is a safe assumption). It must never form loops between neighbor gateways and must suppress loops between non-neighbors, and no loop may last longer than that timeout. Control traffic must not significantly disrupt normal operation, and local changes must not disrupt remote areas.

Resource demands must grow in a controlled way as the network grows. A default gateway is strongly discouraged as a way to shrink the routing database, and if used at all it should only help discover routes. The memo places no restriction on the type of algorithm or metric, but the size of the routing database must not exceed a constant times the number of nodes times the mean connectivity.
sections.plainLanguage: If one road closes, traffic has to find a new way fast, and it must never go around in circles. The memo sets a deadline of about a minute for fixing that.

sections.title: Operation and Maintenance
sections.content:
Gateways are often run as a system by an organization that operates them and resolves link problems with the carriers. The control site may not even be attached to the network it watches. The memo sets these requirements.

  • Each gateway must work as a stand-alone device for local hardware maintenance, with diagnostics runnable from on-site tools only.
  • It must be possible to reboot and dump the gateway manually from the control site, and every gateway must have a watchdog timer that either reboots it or signals a remote site if the software does not reset it periodically.
  • A mechanism must accumulate traffic statistics, preferably retrieved by periodic requests from the control site using a datagram protocol based on UDP or HMP.
  • Exception reports (traps) should be sent immediately to the control site, batched when possible.
  • Link and node status must be displayed continuously at the control site.

Full transport services such as TCP are called ill-advised just to reboot a gateway or collect statistics. The preferred control agent is a user program in a standard environment such as Unix, and specialized host hardware is strongly discouraged. Direct remote control, where the gateway itself supports TCP or UDP, is preferred over an indirect approach using proprietary protocols, though either is acceptable.
sections.plainLanguage: Because nobody sits next to a gateway all day, it needs a watchdog that restarts it if it freezes and a way for helpers far away to check on it and report problems.
